summary: Defines a SIP extension for sending geographic location information from one SIP entity to another. It supports passing location end to end and also routing decisions by intermediaries based on where the target is. It was later updated by RFC 8262 and RFC 8787.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6442 defines how Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) messages carry a target's location, either directly or through a location URI. It also gives the sender control over whether intermediaries may inspect that location to route a request.

subtitle: How SIP messages carry location and control whether intermediaries may route on it.

tldr.problem: SIP had no standard way to convey a target's geographic location end to end or let intermediaries make routing decisions based on that location.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Geolocation, Geolocation-Routing, and Geolocation-Error headers plus a 424 response. Location can be included in a message or referenced by a URI.
tldr.outcome: Location-based routing is permitted only when the sender indicates yes; absence means no. RFC 6442 was later updated by RFC 8262 and RFC 8787.

today: RFC 6442 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 8262 and RFC 8787. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Location in SIP Messages
sections.content:
Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) conveys geographic location from a Target to a Location Recipient. A Target can be a user agent, person, router, or another entity; the sender of the SIP request is not necessarily the Target.

The RFC defines three header fields: Geolocation identifies location information, Geolocation-Routing controls permission to route using it, and Geolocation-Error reports location-specific problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP request can carry information about where a target is. Any intermediary that inspects that information also counts as a recipient of the location.

sections.title: Location by Value or by Reference
sections.content:
Location by value places a Location Object in the SIP message body. Location by reference puts a URI in the request; the recipient follows that URI to retrieve the location from a Location Server.

A SIP intermediary may simply forward the request, or it may inspect location to choose a route or check whether the location is acceptable. If it rejects a request and provides a replacement location, it is responsible for the location information it inserted.
sections.plainLanguage: The location can travel inside the SIP message, or the message can carry an address where it can be retrieved. An intermediary may forward the request or use the location when the sender permits it.

sections.title: The Geolocation Header
sections.content:
The Geolocation header contains one or more location URIs in angle brackets. A cid: URI points to a body part in the same message; other supported URI schemes identify a resource to retrieve.

The header must contain at least one location value, and each value must relate to the original Target. An intermediary SHOULD NOT add a location when one already exists and SHOULD NOT change or delete existing values.
sections.plainLanguage: The Geolocation header tells a recipient where to find one or more location objects. A URI can point to a body part in the message or to a resource that must be retrieved.

sections.title: Permission to Route on Location
sections.content:
Geolocation-Routing: yes allows downstream intermediaries to use location in routing decisions. The value no means intermediaries MUST NOT inspect an included location or retrieve one from a URI for routing.

If the header is absent, the recipient must treat it as no. A no value is a request about intermediary behavior, not a security mechanism; the SIP request can still be processed and forwarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can allow intermediaries to use location when routing a request. If the permission header is missing, the default is no.

sections.title: Bad Location Responses
sections.content:
The 424 (Bad Location Information) response rejects a request because its location is malformed, unsuitable, or could not be retrieved. It MUST include a Geolocation-Error header and MUST NOT be sent for a request with no Geolocation header.

Error ranges indicate whether the recipient cannot process the location, needs permission, or could not retrieve it. The RFC recommends limiting repeated requests for additional location information and limiting URI retrieval attempts.
sections.plainLanguage: A recipient can reject a request when its location information cannot be used and report the reason with an error code. The protocol also recommends limits on repeated rejection and retrieval attempts.

sections.title: Privacy, Security, and Status
sections.content:
The RFC treats location as sensitive information. A user or other Rule Maker decides who can add it and which access rules apply. The document discusses protection through S/MIME, TLS, or authenticated retrieval by reference, each with different limits for intermediaries that need to inspect location.

RFC 6442 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 8262 and RFC 8787. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.
sections.plainLanguage: Location is private, and access should follow the rules set by the person responsible for it. RFC 8262 and RFC 8787 later updated this Proposed Standard.
